tx.t: In this talk I will explain what psychologists know about memory and how students can use it. In eighteen eighty-five, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve.
He found that people forget roughly half of new material within an hour if they do not review it. In nineteen fifty-six, George Miller suggested that short-term memory holds about seven items.
Reviewing material at increasing intervals, which is called spaced repetition, helps to move it into long-term memory. Testing yourself is more effective than simply reading your notes again.
A good night of sleep after studying helps to store what you have learned.

tx.t: In this lecture I will talk about the Great Wall of China. The wall was not built at one time. Different rulers built and rebuilt sections over more than two thousand years.

The first emperor of China, Qin Shi Huang, joined earlier walls together around two hundred and twenty-one BC. Most of the wall that tourists visit today was built in the Ming dynasty, from stone and brick.

A survey in two thousand and twelve measured all its sections at more than twenty-one thousand kilometres. It is a popular story that the wall can be seen from space with the naked eye, but this is not true.

In eighteen forty-eight, the population was about five thousand. Over the next fifty years it grew to twenty-seven thousand.
Then things changed, because the railway came and brought cheaper goods from the cities. As a result, many small traders went out of business.

tx.t: This lecture is about the short history of the internet. The first network, ARPANET, linked four American research sites in nineteen sixty-nine.

In nineteen seventy-one, Ray Tomlinson sent the first email between computers and chose the at sign for addresses. Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working at CERN, invented the World Wide Web at the end of the nineteen eighties.

The web and the internet are not the same thing: the internet is the network, and the web is one service that runs on it. Google was founded in nineteen ninety-eight by two students at Stanford University.
Today, more than five billion people use the internet.

qs.q: How many sites did ARPANET first link? ____

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Fenwick. It began in twenty thirteen with two hundred and eight bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by thirty-nine per cent, and on a busy day there were more than thirty-one thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: too few bikes in the hills. The council solved it with a van that moves bikes uphill every morning.
Today, a ride costs one pounds thirty for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

tx.t: This lecture looks at the history and the future of electric cars. Electric vehicles are older than many people think. The first ones appeared in the eighteen thirties.
Around the year nineteen hundred, more than a quarter of the cars on American roads were electric. Petrol cars then became cheaper and could travel further, so electric cars almost disappeared.

Modern electric cars use lithium-ion batteries, which store more energy for their weight. Their main advantage is that they produce no exhaust gases while driving, though making the batteries does cause pollution.

tx.t: In today's lecture we will study volcanoes and the damage they can do. There are around one thousand three hundred and fifty potentially active volcanoes in the world.
About three quarters of them lie around the Pacific Ocean, in an area called the Ring of Fire. In the year seventy-nine, the eruption of Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman town of Pompeii.

In eighteen fifteen, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted so violently that the following year became known as the year without a summer. The ash from large eruptions can block sunlight and cool the whole planet for a year or more.
Scientists measure small earthquakes and gas emissions to try to predict eruptions.

By twenty ten, the number had risen to four hundred and fifty-one pairs, which shows that careful management can work.
